<image-desc>The Google logo is featured at the top of the page in its multi-colored serif typeface.</image-desc>

This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world's books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the public domain <note>A legal status where a work is no longer protected by intellectual property laws and is free for anyone to use.</note>. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that's often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other marginalia <note>Handwritten notes or marks made in the margins of a book by previous readers or librarians.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file - a reminder of this book's long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying <note>The use of software scripts or "bots" to automatically download or search large amounts of data.</note>.

We also ask that you:

+ **Make non-commercial use of the files** We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ **Refrain from automated querying** Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google's system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition <note>Often abbreviated as OCR; the process of converting images of typed or handwritten text into machine-encoded text.</note> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ **Maintain attribution** The Google "watermark" you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ **Keep it legal** Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can't offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book's appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

## About Google Book Search

Google's mission is to organize the world's information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world's books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. THE conversion of the various <term>Teutonic races</term><note>A historical term for Germanic peoples, including groups like the Goths, Franks, and Saxons.</note> which conquered and occupied the continental provinces of the <term>Roman Empire of the West</term><note>The western half of the Roman Empire, which faced political collapse in the 5th century as these tribes moved into its territories.</note> is distinguished not only by the ease with which it was achieved, but by the steady loyalty with which the victorious tribes held fast to the new religion they had embraced. Many causes contributed toward this result; the intruding <term>barbarians</term><note>The Romans used this term for any foreigners who did not speak Greek or Latin; here, it refers to the invading Germanic tribes.</note> did not displace the existing population who lived under the laws and religion of the imperial city. Instead, they lived among them as joint owners of the land—though they took much of it for themselves at the expense of the original inhabitants—while at the same time refusing to interfere with the established local laws and religious practices. As a natural consequence of this arrangement, the more "civilized" Roman population quickly began to exert a powerful influence over their fierce conquerors, who were inevitably moved

[...the pagan leaders took] the field on the score of national enmity; Edwin and <term>Penda</term><note>The powerful pagan King of Mercia who resisted the spread of Christianity in central England.</note> encountered each other at Heathfield, where the Northumbrian king fell with the greater part of his army, and with him fell, at least for a season, the prosperity of the Church, which from the date of his own conversion he had zealously promoted. <term>Paulinus</term><note>One of the Roman missionaries sent by Pope Gregory the Great; he was the first Bishop of York.</note>, Archbishop of York, was driven from the scene of his hitherto fruitful labours, while the successors of Edwin in the two Northumbrian kingdoms, <term>Deira</term><note>The southern part of Northumbria, centered around modern Yorkshire.</note> and <term>Bernicia</term><note>The northern part of Northumbria, extending into what is now Scotland.</note>, with all their people, at once lapsed into <term>idolatry</term><note>A return to the worship of the old Germanic gods like Woden (Odin).</note>, hoping thereby to propitiate the conquerors. In the days of <term>Edwin</term><note>The first Christian king of Northumbria, killed by Penda and Cædwalla.</note> the Gospel had come to Northumbria direct from <term>Rome</term><note>Specifically, the Gregorian mission sent by the Pope.</note>, for <term>Paulinus</term><note>The Roman missionary who first baptized King Edwin.</note> was the friend and companion of <term>St. Augustine</term><note>The first Archbishop of Canterbury, sent to convert the Anglo-Saxons in 597.</note>, but Oswald, who had himself received Christianity from the monks of <term>Iona</term><note>A monastery founded by St. Columba on a small island in the Inner Hebrides, which became a center of Gaelic monasticism.</note>, naturally sought their aid in the work of <term>reconversion</term><note>Returning the population to the Christian faith after their lapse into paganism following Edwin's death.</note>. A band of missionaries, with <term>Aidan</term><note>St. Aidan, an Irish monk from Iona known for his asceticism and his ability to walk everywhere to preach to the poor.</note> as their bishop, obeyed the royal summons. They were received with universal exultation, and Oswald bade their leader choose any spot in the kingdom which might please him best as his <term>episcopal seat</term><note>The official center or cathedral city of a bishop's authority.</note>. After Cuthbert’s death, **Eadbert** ruled the **see** <term>see: The official seat of a bishop's jurisdiction and authority.</term> of Lindisfarne. His successor (in the year 698) was **Eadfrith**, to whose skill we owe that unrivalled piece of Saxon penmanship known as the **Lindisfarne** or **Durham Gospels**. This task, we know with tolerable certainty, was finished before his appointment to the see, and possibly the book might have been begun as a gift to the saint during his life-time, which was afterwards offered by the writer at his shrine. Bishop Eadfrith seems to have been inspired by zealous affection towards his predecessor, for he put the oratory of **Farne Island** into repair, and at his special bidding **Bede** <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 673–735), a monk and scholar at Jarrow, widely considered the greatest writer of the Anglo-Saxon age.</note> wrote his well-known lives in prose and verse of St. Cuthbert. St. Cuthbert, it is hinted, might have overlooked the **venial sin** <term>venial sin: In Christian theology, a lesser sin that does not result in complete spiritual death or separation from God.</term> of curiosity had not brother John been further guilty of sacrilege, in that he had handled the sacred volume without wearing his alb; and so far from having purged his soul by previous fasting, as he was in duty bound, had come greasy from his dinner, not so much as tarrying to wash his hands. Speedy punishment overtakes the culprit in the form of a sharp fit of illness, minutely described by Reginald, who does not spare his reader a single symptom. All remedies are in vain till the offender openly confesses his fault, and begs St. Cuthbert's forgiveness, when at once he

“The other letters in these ornamental pages vary from half an inch to an inch and half; they are greatly diversified in their forms, scarcely any two being alike. An extensive series of them is given by Astle <note>Thomas Astle (1735–1803), a noted English antiquary and paleographer who wrote 'The Origin and Progress of Writing'.</note>, who considers that some are identical with those of the Phoenicians, Pelasgians <note>A term used by ancient Greek writers to refer to the populations that preceded the Greeks in the Aegean region.</note>, Etruscans <note>A powerful civilization in ancient Italy, prior to the rise of Rome.</note>, Greeks, Romans, and others, ‘and that this alphabet alone bears strong testimony that the letters used by our Saxon ancestors are derived from the Phoenician, the Etruscan, and the Greek letters *through the medium of the Roman*.’”

Professor Westwood <note>John Obadiah Westwood (1805–1893), an entomologist and archaeologist who specialized in the artistic style of early medieval manuscripts.</note>, however, does not entirely subscribe to the opinion expressed by Astle; he observes, that “many of these letters are the result of the fancy of the calligrapher <note>A professional scribe or beautiful-writer.</note>,” and considers that “others must be referred to other sources than the Roman alphabet.” He especially points out that the capital **M**, “singularly formed as it mostly is of three perpendicular strokes united across the middle with one horizontal bar, or occasionally with two bars, is not to be found in any Roman inscriptions, so far at least as I have been able to observe, but, on the contrary, is evidently of Phoenician or Pelasgic origin.

In addition to the previous description, the Editor has also been provided by J. B. Waring, Esq. <note>John Burley Waring, a 19th-century architect and scholar of decorative arts.</note>, with the following observations upon the style of decoration shown in the Lindisfarne Gospels. Mr. Waring remarks of our manuscript book <note>original Latin: "Codex"</note>, that, “with the exception of the Book of Kells, this is the most elaborate and beautiful surviving example of the style of ornament which distinguishes the Celtic school, many examples of which are still preserved throughout Europe. Professor Westwood, in his valuable *Sacred Pictorial Palaeography* <note>original Latin: "Palæographia Sacra Pictoria"; a study of ancient handwriting and manuscript art.</note>, describes the characteristics of the school as consisting of:

1st, one or more ribbons woven together diagonally but evenly <note>original: "symmetrically interlaced"</note>, forming an endless variety of patterns; 

2nd, one, two, or three slender spiral lines coiling one within another until they meet in the center of the circle, their opposite ends going off to other circles; 

3rd, a vast variety of lizard-like <note>original: "lacertine"</note> animals and birds, strangely thinned <note>original: "attenuated"</note> and coiled one within another, their tails, tongues, and crests <note>original: "top-knots"</note> forming long narrow ribbons woven together irregularly; 

4th, a series of diagonal lines, forming various kinds of patterns similar to Chinese fretwork. 

These ornaments are generally introduced into small sections <note>original: "compartments"</note>, a number of which are arranged so as to form the large initial letters and borders, or mosaic-like pages <note>original: "tessellated pages"; these are often referred to by modern scholars as "carpet pages."</note>, with which the finest manuscripts are decorated.’

“It is these large pages of pure decoration which lend such an attractive interest to the Book of Saint Cuthbert’s Gospels <note>A common historical name for the Lindisfarne Gospels, as they were believed to have been written for the saint.</note>; the extraordinary delicacy, fineness, and

->### PRELIMINARY REMARKS.<-
->f<-

The complexity of the <term>lacertine<gloss>lizard-like or serpentine</gloss></term> lines, the perfect reproduction and repetition of various portions, bear witness to a marvelous care in tracing, and an exquisite sense of beauty in decoration, which rivals the most elaborate and finest productions of the Eastern masters of the art. The original source of the coiled and spiral work, which forms so distinguishing a characteristic of the style, may have been the ancient Greek scroll, which, drawn in to a point and then out, trailed backwards, forwards and sideways, and filled in with scroll-like or spiral forms of the same nature, has produced a style of linear ornamentation quite peculiar to the Celtic school. This, combined with the lizard-like forms before alluded to, renders it a distinctive style. That style bears, we think, traces of its formative process on the face of it, and appears to contain several features of Byzantine origin <note>Artistic styles from the Eastern Roman Empire, centered in Constantinople.</note>, founded on ancient Greek suggestions; transplanted to Ireland, these <term>motifs<gloss>recurring decorative patterns or themes</gloss></term> became naturalized, and were developed and finally molded by native artists into a distinct and perfect system, forming thus a style *in itself* <note>original Latin: "per se"</note>, minute, complex, delicate in outline and in color, complete in all its parts, and harmonious in its general effect.

And a further proof of this Western origin, combined with lingering reminiscences of the East, is to be found in the writing inscribed above each of the Evangelists; thus in the picture of St. Matthew, we have an angel (with <term>nimbus<gloss>a halo or radiant circle surrounding the head of a holy person</gloss></term>) blowing a horn, and the words "**image of a man**" <note>original Latin: "imago hominis"</note>; above the Saint himself, "**Saint Matthew**" <note>original Greek/Latin hybrid: "O agios Mattheus"</note>. In this page also is shewn a human figure, half hidden by a curtain, which would appear to represent God himself in the act of dictation to the apostle: a representation which would never have been tolerated in the Eastern Church; and another example of which, Mr. Westwood <note>John Obadiah Westwood (1805–1893), a famous paleographer and archaeologist who studied these manuscripts.</note> informs us, is to be seen in the Royal Library at Copenhagen. It is most unusual to find God the Father thus represented in early Western manuscripts, although we know that in after ages this violation of the express command of the Deity became common in the pictorial and carved art of mediæval Europe. Above St. Mark is depicted a lion (with halo) blowing a horn, and beneath it "**image of a lion**" <note>original Latin: "imago leonis"</note>; over the Evangelist is the inscription "**Saint Mark**" <note>original: "O agius Marcus"</note>. The <term>glosser<gloss>a scholar who adds translations or explanations between the lines of a text</gloss></term> Aldred, in entries he has made at the foot of the Gospels of St. Matthew and St. John, supplies the date to which Mr. Waring refers, by recording the names of his fellow-labourers in the production of the Codex. The foot-note affixed to St. Matthew is short, and may thus be translated:

> Thou, O living God, bear in mind Eadfrith, and Æthilwald, and Billfrith, and Aldred the sinner. These four, with God’s help, were employed<note>1</note> upon this book.

The entry at the close of St. John is longer, and affords interesting details:

> Eadfrith, bishop over the church of Lindisfarne, first wrote this book in (honour of) God and St. Cuthbert, and all the company of saints in the island; and Æthilwald, bishop of Lindisfarne, made an outer cover, and adorned it as he was well able; and Billfrith, the <term>anchorite<gloss>a religious hermit; in this context, a skilled metalworker living in seclusion</gloss></term>, he wrought the metal work of the ornaments on the outside thereof, and decked it with gold and with gems, overlaid also with silver, unalloyed metal. And Aldred, an unworthy and most miserable priest, by the help of God and St. Cuthbert, over-glossed the same in English, and associated himself with the three parts <note>This likely refers to Aldred joining his own work of translation to the work of the three men who preceded him: the scribe, the binder, and the goldsmith.</note>. Madden provides 950 as the approximate date and identifies Aldred as the same person who added the interlinear translations <note>glosses</note> to the Durham Ritual <note>A 10th-century book of prayers and rites used at Durham Cathedral</note>. Two scribes have been employed on our Gospels; the first portion was written by some person appointed by Aldred, and probably under his dictation; the second hand in red ink, which we know to have been Aldred’s own handwriting <note>autograph</note>, is distinguished by the v-shaped letter for 'u' and 'p', and by certain spelling habits, such as *bloedsia* <gloss>to bless</gloss>, and the use of *gi* for *ge* in the inseparable prefix; these forms are equally characteristic of the Ritual. According to this hypothesis, the “promotion and dignity,” which seem to have been the object of his aspirations, were not denied to our translator, who reappears in 970 as Aldred the provost <note>a high-ranking administrative officer in the church</note>, second only in dignity in the church of St. Cuthbert to its bishop, Ælfsig. He is recorded as a fellow-traveler when that prelate accompanies Kenneth, the King of Scots, to the court of Edgar, King of Wessex <note>Edgar the Peaceful, reigned 959–975</note>.

->II.<-

The establishment of a Christian community in Rome cannot be looked upon as the commencement of Latin Christianity, for the first converts in the Imperial city, the men to whom St. Paul addressed his arguments and exhortations, though attracted to the new faith, partly from Judaism, and partly from heathenism, were alike Greeks in language, were alike aliens to the blood and speech of Latium <note>The region of central Italy where the Latin language and Roman culture originated.</note>. To this fact the literary monuments of the early Roman Church bear unmistakable testimony; the *Clementine Recognitions*, the *Shepherd of Hermas*, and the *Philosophumena* of Hippolytus <note>Three foundational works of early Christian literature; their original composition in Greek proves that the early Church in Rome was linguistically Greek rather than Latin.</note>, all written by members of the Roman Church, and intended by their

authors, primarily at least, to exercise an influence upon that body, appear in Greek as the language prevalent among the public for whose edification the above-named works were designed. The Old Testament in its Alexandrian translation <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible from the 3rd century BCE.</note>, and the New Testament in its original language <note>Greek</note> were as intelligible to the faithful on the banks of the Tiber <note>The river that runs through Rome.</note>, as to the congregations of Corinth and Antioch; nor was it till the middle of the third century that the Church of Rome had completed its momentous transformation from Greek to Latin nationality.

But during the long period in which the Latin element was leavening the Roman Church, the Gospel had been communicated to regions where the speech and culture of Rome were predominant, to Spain and North Africa; and for many ages Carthage <note>A powerful ancient city in modern-day Tunisia and a major center of early Christianity.</note> bore a part in developing the polity <term>polity: the organized structure or government of a church</term> and doctrine of the Western Church, scarcely less important than that taken by Rome herself. To these more remote branches of the Catholic Church <note>original: "Catholic Church," referring to the "universal" body of Christian believers at the time.</note> a Latin version of the Scriptures was indispensable, and it was not long ere this want was supplied, but the particulars of the work, the exact or even approximate date, and the name and country of its author are unknown.

Critics are less agreed upon the date than the birthplace of this translation; it was probably made towards the middle of the second century; and to judge by the principle that demand calls forth supply, it may be concluded with a fair amount of probability that it issued from the Church of Carthage, at that time the most numerous and flourishing among the Christian communities speaking the Latin tongue. counting the congregations of Lyons <note>original: "Lugdunum," a major Roman city in Gaul, now modern-day Lyons, France</note> and Vienne <note>A city in southeastern France that was an early center of Christianity</note> which were Greek, had scarcely emerged from infancy. As, however, Christianity became more generally diffused throughout the Western divisions of the Empire, the version of the Scriptures adopted by the African Church met with universal acceptance, and under the title of the “Italic,” <note>The *Vetus Itala*, or "Old Latin" version of the Bible used before St. Jerome's Vulgate became standard.</note> it became to the Churches of the West a standard as authoritative as was the Alexandrian version <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> for those of the East, from which indeed, and not from the original Hebrew, the Old Testament was translated into Latin. Unfortunately however, the Italic translation, originally released without any direct and formal sanction from church authority, and subsequently unprotected by the careful and jealous oversight of Christian scholars, was in process of time deformed by a multitude of corruptions, caused partly by the errors of scribes, partly by the whims of individuals. “For in the early times of the Faith, whenever a Greek copy came into possession of one who fancied himself a tolerable expert in both languages, he boldly took upon him to interpret.” <note>original Latin footnote: Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book 2, Chapter 11; cited in De Wette’s *Textbook*, page 79.</note> The inconveniences of this irregular and unauthorized interference at length became intolerable, the current copies of the Italic text were pronounced untrustworthy by all competent judges, and various means were employed to remedy this evil. At first the faulty copies, chiefly African, were sent to Italy, there to be compared with the Greek, and to receive some improvement in their Latinity <term>Latinity: the use of style, grammar, and vocabulary characteristic of the Latin language</term>; this procedure, however, conducted without method and without due supervision, proved inadequate to accomplish the end

---

¹ Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine* 2. 11. in De Wette *Textbook*, p. 79.

Numerous specimens of this kind of <term>recension</term> <note>A scholarly revision of a text based on the careful comparison of different manuscript versions.</note> exist in the libraries of Europe; the most important of these are printed in the collections of Sabatier and Blanchini <note>Pierre Sabatier and Giuseppe Bianchini were 18th-century scholars who famously collected and edited fragments of the "Old Latin" Bible versions that predated the Vulgate.</note>, and are not without value in the criticism of the sacred text. They are particularly useful for testing the character of those forms of the old Latin version which for many ages held their ground, despite the gradually but surely increasing reputation of St. Jerome’s translation. 

For this Father <note>A "Church Father" refers to influential Christian theologians and scholars from the early centuries of the Church.</note>, whose learning equalled his abilities and energy, applied himself for many years to the task of presenting the Latin-speaking world with a faithful rendering in their own tongue of the entire Bible. He translated the Old and New Testaments respectively from their original Hebrew and Greek sources. His version of the books of the Jewish <term>canon</term> <note>The collection of books officially recognized as sacred scripture.</note> is an independent work; however, in his treatment of the New Testament, he confined himself to a thorough revision of the common "Italic" version then in use. 

This great performance, though undertaken under the protection of the Roman Church, was but coldly received by Jerome’s contemporaries. Even St. Augustine, while acknowledging its value and making use of it in his own commentaries on the Scriptures, hesitated to sanction its adoption in the public services of the Church. Among other reasons for his reluctance on this point, he alleged that the abandonment of the <term>Alexandrian version</term> <note>The Septuagint, a Greek translation of the Old Testament used by the early Greek-speaking Church.</note>—which would be implied by officially adopting Jerome’s version—would give support to a suspicion of disagreement between the Greek and Latin-speaking branches of the Church. Jerome himself found the "Italic" text of the Gospels to be thoroughly untrustworthy, and regarding this, he remarks in the preface to his amended translation of those books:

> “If any dependence is to be placed upon the Latin copies, let an answer be given to the question: upon which of them?” <note>original Latin: "Si qua enim Latinis exemplaribus fides est adhibenda, respondeant quibus." Jerome is pointing out that because there were so many different, conflicting Latin translations, none could be trusted without a return to the original Greek.</note>

for there are almost as many forms of the text as there are transcripts of it¹.”

For two centuries the *Hieronymic translation* <note>The translation produced by St. Jerome (known as Hieronymus in Latin) between 382 and 405 AD.</note> had to make its way among the Latin clergy simply upon its own merits, till Gregory I. adopted it as the official Bible of the Roman Church, a decisive step towards its exaltation to the same rank by all the national Churches to whom the <term>Apostolic See</term> <note>The office and jurisdiction of the Pope in Rome.</note> was the model and directress. The very pontiff, however, who pronounced so decided a verdict in favour of the *Vulgate* <note>From the Latin 'editio vulgata' meaning 'common edition'; the standard Latin Bible.</note>, did not abide consistently by his own judgment. In the preface to his *commentary on Job* he writes, “The *New Version* (i. e. *Jerome's*) is the one upon which my explanations are based, but as each case to be proved requires, I cite texts at one time from the New, at another from the Old: to the end that, since the Apostolic See, (over which I preside by Divine ordinance,) makes use of both, my labour in this undertaking may be supported by both².” Gregory’s laxity in this matter was followed in all the Churches of the West; and the *Old Italic* <note>The 'Vetus Latina' or 'Old Latin' versions that existed before Jerome's revision.</note>, though lowered in estimation, was by no means supplanted³. arose a fresh source of corruption to both texts, for where learning was at so low an ebb, and criticism hardly dreamed of, hybrid transcripts were at length circulated, in some of which the *Hieronymic* <note>The translation produced by St. Jerome (Hieronymus) in the late 4th century.</note>, in others the *Italic* <note>The 'Vetus Latina' or 'Old Latin' versions that preceded Jerome's work.</note> element prevailed, not to speak of passages interpolated from one Evangelist into another, and of clerical blunders utterly subversive of the meaning of the places in which they are committed¹. From the time of Charlemagne to the end of the sixteenth century various attempts were made to bring back Jerome’s text to its pristine integrity, and this became an object of pressing urgency for that part of Christendom which adhered to the Roman See, after that decree of the <term>Tridentine Council</term> <note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563), which established the Vulgate as the official Bible of the Catholic Church.</note> which raised the *Vulgate* <note>The standard Latin Bible translation.</note> to a normal and decisive authority. Sixtus V. and Clement VIII. undertook the task of presenting the Catholic world with a corrected edition of the *Vulgate*, and the <term>recension</term> <note>A critical revision or edited version of a text.</note> put forth by the latter pontiff (1592) has since his time been received by the Latin Church as a document against which no appeal is valid, even though made to the original texts. Catholic as well as Protestant scholars are aware that this <term>recension</term> does not adhere strictly to Jerome’s translation, though it is doubtless vastly superior to all the editions it superseded; a critical revision of the *Vulgate*, founded upon the numerous old and authentic copies still in existence, is greatly to be desired.

But to return to the Lindisfarne and Rushworth Gospels. These **MSS.** <note>abbreviation for manuscripts</note> were written at a period when all the causes of textual corruption abovenamed were in full operation, and they are consequently not free from wrong readings of every description; the Lindisfarne Codex <note>A "codex" is an ancient book composed of handwritten pages bound together.</note> is by far the more correct of the two, nor are its mistakes by any means so glaring as those perpetrated by Macregol <note>The scribe of the Rushworth Gospels, also known as the "Gospels of Macregol."</note>. Still it presents errors which we should hardly look for from the pen of so accomplished a scribe as Eadfrith <note>The Bishop of Lindisfarne (698–721 AD) credited with writing and illuminating the Lindisfarne Gospels.</note>, a man who lived in the palmy days of Northumbrian scholarship, at a time when Archbishop Theodore <note>Theodore of Tarsus (602–690 AD), who significantly reformed English education and the Church.</note> had, as Hickes <note>George Hickes (1642–1715), a pioneering scholar of Anglo-Saxon and Germanic languages.</note> has remarked, “advanced learning to a great height in the Saxon Churches¹.” A few specimens of its mistakes will satisfy the reader’s curiosity: Luke, ch. i. 27. *a virgin betrothed to a virgin* (should be: to a man)² <note>original Latin: "virginem desponsatã virgo (viro)"</note>; ch. iv. 17. *he found the place where it was written* <note>original Latin: "invenit loco ubi scriptum erat"</note>; ch. vi. 8. *a great* (should be: hand) *withered* <note>original Latin: "magnum (manum) aridam"</note>, ver. 20. *power from him went out* <note>The scribe used a plural verb "exiebant" for a singular subject; original Latin: "virtus de illo exiebant"</note>, ver. 26. *prophets* (should be: false-prophets) <note>original Latin: "prophetas (pseudo-prophetas)"</note>, ver. 37. *do not be condemned* <note>original Latin: "nolite condemnari"</note>, ver. 49. *upon the rock* (should be: the earth) <note>original Latin: "supra petram (terram)"</note>; ch. vii. 28. *not among* (should be: greater among) <note>original Latin: "non inter (major inter)"</note>, and in the same verse *to whom* (should be: who) <note>original Latin: "cui (qui)"</note>.

means a favourable specimen; barbarous spelling, flagrant violations of grammar, omissions and interpolations are salient characteristics of this <term>MS.</term> <note>abbreviation for manuscript</note>, which exhibits errors of such magnitude and absurdity as would seem possible only in the case of a person ignorant of the Latin language, and writing from a defective memory. It presents those orthographical <note>spelling</note> peculiarities which appear common to the ancient Irish manuscripts described in the *Palæographia Sacra* <note>A mid-19th century reference work on ancient manuscripts by Mary Anne Wyatt and J.O. Westwood.</note>. The single vowel, especially when followed by another vowel¹, is preferred to the <term>diphthong</term> <note>a sound formed by the combination of two vowels in a single syllable</note>; <term>itacism</term> <note>a linguistic shift where various vowels and diphthongs are pronounced like the "ee" in "feet"</note> prevails; and there is a marked inclination to open vowel-sounds, as *mormor* <note>original Latin: "murmur"</note>; **v** occurs for **b** and **f**, and **f** or **p** for **ph**, as in *farisseis* <note>original Latin: "pharisaeis" (Pharisees)</note> and *pilipus* <note>original Latin: "philippus" (Philip)</note>; **b**, **p**, and **d**, **t** are interchangeable. The use of **ss** is capricious, such as *quassi* <note>original Latin: "quasi" (as if)</note> and *misus* <note>original Latin: "missus" (sent)</note>; **bp** or **dp** are joined for **pp**, and **dt** for **tt**. **Ch** is used for **c** and **h** (*channa* <note>original: "Cana"</note>, *abracham* <note>original: "Abraham"</note>). The <term>aspirate</term> <note>the 'h' sound</note> is frequently omitted, thus in John ii. 9 we have *they were golden*² <note>original Latin: "auri erant," a mistake for "haurierant" (they had drawn water)</note>. The division of this word also affords a specimen of remarkable ignorance in our scribe, who constantly confounds the <term>inflexional termination</term> <note>the ending of a word that indicates its grammatical case or tense</note> of verbs with the <term>verb substantive</term> <note>the verb "to be"</note>; in the same chapter, verse 24, he writes *us was* <note>original Latin: "nos esset," a mistake for "nosset" (he knew)</note>. But these are venial <note>minor or excusable</note> errors compared with others indulged in by Macregol, who occasionally varies his text by original blunders of the finest Milesian <note>A historical term referring to the Irish; the author is implying these are characteristically Irish mistakes.</note> flavour. In John iv. a repetition appears of the 16th verse and most of the 17th; *he says* <note>original Latin: "dicit"</note> occurs twice, and the scribe, having completed his page with the second, turned the leaf, and started afresh from the first *he says*;

In chapter 7, verse 8, he adds to this sin of commission one of omission by leaving out an entire line in his transcription; in chapter 8, verse 53, where the text should read "you have a demon. I will inflict but one more instance of Macregol's shortcomings upon the reader, and that by way of illustrating the description of various readings which are actually obtainable when crass ignorance and stupidity meet in a scribe. In John 6:53, we have: "unless you have eaten his flesh to give to be eaten, Jesus therefore said to them, Amen [truly] sons of man, and if you drink his blood you shall not have life in you" <note>original Latin: "nisi manducaveritis carnem suam dare ad manducandum, dixit ergo eis Ihs, amen filii hominis, et biberitis ejus sanguinem non habebitis in vobis vitam"</note>¹.

# ST. MATTHEW.

In instances where the early Latin manuscripts <term>codices <note>Plural of codex; ancient manuscript books, specifically those of the Bible.</note></term> published by Giuseppe Bianchini <note>An 18th-century Italian scholar known for his work on the "Evangeliarium Quadruplex," a comparison of early Latin Gospel manuscripts.</note> align with the variations found in the Lindisfarne and Rushworth manuscripts <note>original abbreviation: "MSS."</note> when compared to the <term>Vulgate <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible that became the standard version for the Catholic Church.</note></term>, this agreement is noted with the letters L. (for the Lindisfarne Gospels) and R. (for the Rushworth Gospels). Minor differences that appear even when Bianchini’s texts largely agree with these two manuscripts are noted in the footnotes.

<meta>This page transitions from a detailed technical table of textual variants in the Gospel of Matthew to the formal preface (Prolegomena). While the previous page provided a verse-by-verse comparison of ancient Latin and Anglo-Saxon manuscripts, this section provides historical context for why a complete Anglo-Saxon Bible did not exist, focusing on the influence of Latin-speaking leaders and the education system of the early English Church.</meta>

<page-num>c</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

### III.

The administration of the early English <note>original: "Anglo-Saxon"</note> Church by foreign bishops <note>original: "alien prelates"</note>, the great prominence given to the study of Latin in the system of monastic education established by Theodore <note>Theodore of Tarsus (602–690 AD), the Archbishop of Canterbury who transformed English education by introducing Greek and Latin studies.</note>, and the very small number of laymen whose thirst for knowledge or religious devotion would lead them to learn to read their own language, fairly accounts for the lack of a complete Old English version of the Holy Scriptures. A large summary <note>original: "copious epitome"</note> of the first five books of Moses <note>The Pentateuch</note>, the first two historical books, and Job, together with the Psalms <note>The Psalter</note> (partly in the form of a poetic version), comprised the whole of the Old Testament placed within the reach of that small class of men who, though literate in their own tongue, lacked the scholarly skill of Latin. Of the New Testament, only the Four Gospels were translated into Old English; and while the accuracy of this version gives it great value for scholars investigating the sacred text, its directness, its power, and its grammatical precision rank it among the most noteworthy...

---

->¹ **Book-Latin** <note>original: "Boc-Leden"; the Old English term for the Latin language, associated specifically with written learning.</note> became not only an essential skill for the clergy, but also the favorite accomplishment of women in the convents. The treatise **On the Praises of Virginity** <note>original: "De Laudibus Virginitatis"</note>, written by Saint Aldhelm <note>An 8th-century scholar and Bishop of Sherborne.</note> for the abbess Hildelith and her nuns, is written in Latin. We learn from it that the nuns were accustomed to read the first five books of the Bible, the books of the prophets, and the New Testament, along with the commentaries of the Church Fathers in that language. *St. Aldhelm, On the Praises of Virginity, p. 294.*<-

<summary>This preface explains that a complete Old English Bible was never produced because the Church was led by foreign bishops who prioritized Latin education, leaving only the Gospels and parts of the Old Testament available in the native tongue.</summary>
<keywords>Theodore of Tarsus, Book-Latin, Old English Gospels, monastic education, St. Aldhelm, female literacy, Bible translation history</keywords>

--- Page 106 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the history of Old English biblical translations. It concludes a sentence describing the West Saxon Gospels as "monuments of ancient Teutonic literature" and moves into a comparison with the Northumbrian glosses, detailing the cultural decay in Northern England during the Viking Age.</meta>

<page-num>ci</page-num>
<header>### PREFACE <note>original: "PROLEGOMENA"</note></header>

monuments of ancient Germanic <note>original: "Teutonic"</note> literature. The two interlinear translations <note>original: "glosses"</note> now presented for the first time to the public by the Surtees Society <note>A text-publication society founded in 1834 to publish documents relating to the history of Northern England.</note> showcase the Northumbrian dialect <note>original: "North Anglian"</note> in a form that stands in sharp contrast to the West Saxon version mentioned earlier. While the West Saxon version was clearly the work of a master of his own language during its most refined period, these Northumbrian translations were produced by uneducated scribes. They used a common speech that had been degraded by a lack of formal education and at a time when its purity had been destroyed by repeated invasions and foreign settlements.

In the ancient kingdom of Northumbria, both religion and scholarship had been declining for nearly a century before the repeated invasions of the Vikings <note>original: "Northmen"</note>. During those raids, all the literary treasures of the country perished along with the churches and monasteries where they were stored. By the end of the ninth century, the Danish settlers in Northumbria were far more numerous and powerful than the native population. The locals had become demoralized by constant warfare and the influence of the invaders who, although they nominally adopted the Christian faith, still lived and behaved like pagans. Consequently, the country everywhere presented the sad spectacle of a violent and lawless population and a lazy, immoral, and uneducated clergy.

This decline was not limited to northern England; throughout the entire country, the clerical order had fallen into such deep ignorance that it justified the famous complaint of King Alfred the Great <note>Reigned 871–899 AD; he was a major proponent of English literacy.</note>, who wrote:

> “so completely had learning fallen away in England that there were very few [priests] on this side of the Humber who could translate their church services into English, or even translate a...”

<summary>This page explains how Viking invasions and Danish settlements led to a decline in Northumbrian scholarship and religion, resulting in "debased" linguistic forms compared to the more refined West Saxon literature.</summary>
<keywords>Northumbria, Vikings, King Alfred the Great, Northumbrian dialect, West Saxon, Danish settlers, monastic decline, Surtees Society</keywords>

--- Page 107 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the decline of scholarship in Northern England, specifically focusing on the low level of Latin literacy among the clergy which necessitated the creation of interlinear translations.</meta>

<page-num>cii</page-num>

<header>### PREFACE <note>original: "PROLEGOMENA"</note></header>

...letter from Latin into English, and not many, I believe, would be able [to do so] on the other side of the Humber¹."

In a degeneracy of learning among the priests <note>original: "clergy"</note> and monks, so complete that few of them were versed in the Latin <note>original: "sacred idiom of the Western Church"</note> language, some contrivance became necessary for helping them to understand what it was their daily duty to read or to hear. To this end those portions of the Scriptures of most importance for church services <note>original: "liturgical importance"</note>, such as the Gospels and the Book of Psalms <note>original: "Psalter"</note>, were furnished with an **interlinear gloss**. In these, every word of the Latin text was literally, and even slavishly, translated into the common speech <note>original: "vulgar tongue"</note>. This served partly as a translation and partly as a continuous vocabulary list, making it useful not only for public worship but also for teaching the Latin language.

Of this kind of writing, the Old English <note>original: "Saxon"</note> portions of the **Lindisfarne** and **Rushworth Gospels** are very notable examples. The Rushworth Gospels have been dated by Wanley <note>Humfrey Wanley (1672–1726), a pioneering scholar of Anglo-Saxon manuscripts.</note> to the end of the ninth or the beginning of the tenth century. Based on its grammatical forms², it

---

¹ <note>original Anglo-Saxon: "Mē com swīðe oft on gemynd hwilce witan geo wæron geond Angelcyn... ic wēne þ nāht monige begeondan Humbre wæron."</note> "It has very often come to my mind what wise men there were formerly throughout the English nation <note>original: "Angelcyn"</note>, both of religious and secular orders; and how people from abroad sought wisdom and instruction here in this land, and how we now would have to get them from outside if we were to have them. So completely was learning fallen away among the English people that there were very few on this side of the Humber who could understand their divine service in English, or even translate a single letter from Latin into English; and I believe there were not many beyond the Humber." — *Letter of King Alfred, cited in Walker’s Life of Alfred, p. 196.*

² Still the book in question strikingly illustrates the difficulty of fixing any certain date for manuscripts on the mere ground of grammatical precision. That the two scribes of the Rushworth gloss were contemporaries is beyond a doubt, yet the Old English of **Farman** <note>One of the two scribes of the Rushworth Gospels; he was a priest at Harewood.</note>, a man of some cultivation, might at first sight be referred to an earlier period than that of his less educated fellow-worker.

<summary>This page explains the historical necessity of interlinear glosses (word-for-word translations) due to the collapse of Latin literacy among the English clergy, citing King Alfred’s famous lament over the state of learning.</summary>
<keywords>King Alfred the Great, interlinear gloss, Rushworth Gospels, Lindisfarne Gospels, Latin literacy, Old English, Humfrey Wanley, Farman the scribe</keywords>

<page-num>ciii</page-num>

<header>### PREFACE <note>original Latin: "PROLEGOMENA"</note></header>

appears somewhat older than the version of the **Cotton MS** <note>The Lindisfarne Gospels, part of the famous library collected by Sir Robert Cotton.</note>. The date of the latter can be assigned to the middle of the tenth century upon highly probable evidence, which should be set aside only by the production of stronger testimony of the same kind as that which it is intended to refute. Karl Bouterwek <note>A 19th-century German scholar of Old English.</note>, in the learned preface to his reconstruction of the Cotton gloss, among other reasons for assigning it to the first half of the twelfth century¹, insists strongly upon one which especially merits attention. He infers that the version must have been made later than the beginning of the twelfth century, because Simeon of Durham <note>A chronicler and monk who wrote around 1130.</note>, who flourished in 1130, makes no mention of **Aldred** <note>The priest who added the English translation between the lines of the Lindisfarne Gospels.</note> in his record of the persons engaged upon the writing and ornamentation of **St. Cuthbert’s Book** <note>A traditional name for the Lindisfarne Gospels.</note>. Bouterwek argues from this omission that the book could not have been glossed <note>provided with an interlinear translation</note> when Simeon examined it. But it may be observed that a learned churchman like the historian of Durham, who required no translation to supplement his knowledge of the Latin text, would be so far from valuing such an addition to the manuscript that he would likely consider the sacred volume to have suffered desecration by being interpolated with the rude speech of the ignorant common people.

· 1 Bouterwek considers the Cotton gloss as contemporary with the text of **Layamon** <note>The author of 'The Brut', an early Middle English poem.</note>. But the marked difference of forms between the two compositions renders this view untenable. As for example, the breathing sound <note>the aspirate</note> always precedes the *w* in the gloss <note>such as 'hwet'</note>, but follows it in Layamon <note>such as 'what'</note>; the *i-*, used for the forming prefix *ge-* <note>a common prefix in Old English verbs</note>, is universal in the poem, but only occurs once in the gloss (John v. 15), probably as a scribal error; the frequent use in the Gospels of *wutu*, *wutun* <note>meaning 'let us'</note>, and <term>geræfa<note>A local official or 'reeve'.</note></term>; the dative case ending in *-n*, common throughout Layamon, is not found in the gloss. These may serve as specimens of the discrepancies, both in spelling and grammar, which will present themselves on even the most superficial comparison.

<meta>This page continues the technical comparison between the Lindisfarne and Rushworth Gospels, specifically focusing on the linguistic evidence that suggests both translations (glosses) originated from a single source.</meta>

<page-num>civ</page-num>

<header>### PREFACE <note>original Latin: "PROLEGOMENA"</note></header>

Our two glosses <note>The interlinear English translations added between the lines of the Latin text.</note> bear so strong a general resemblance to each other that they have been usually regarded as sister versions; so much would be concluded after a cursory examination, but a closer investigation gives full confirmation to this view. One line of proof especially bears upon this subject. Passages constantly occur where both glosses render the text with verbal identity in so erroneous or so singular a manner, that mere coincidence is out of the question, and the only possible hypothesis is that both glossists drew from a common original. A few instances will suffice to illustrate and to justify the opinion expressed. 

In Mark 6:14, the Lindisfarne manuscript reads *inopinantur* <note>Latin: "they are not expected"</note> and translates it accordingly as "are unsuspected" <note>Old English: *inwoen sint*</note>; the Rushworth manuscript reads *operantur* <note>Latin: "they work"</note>, but gives the same translation as the Lindisfarne. In Mark 6:17, "wife" <note>Latin: *uxorem*</note> is translated as "remnant" or "widow" <note>Old English: *hlaf* in Lindisfarne, *lafe* in Rushworth</note>.¹ In Mark 11:23, "to take up and to cast" <note>Latin: *tollere et mittere*</note> is translated in both manuscripts as "take and send" <note>Old English: *genioma ⁊ sende*</note>. In Mark 13:18, the Latin text of this verse is given incompletely in Lindisfarne but fully in Rushworth, while the translation in Rushworth extends only to as much of the verse as it has in common with Lindisfarne. In John 3:33, "his testimony" <note>Latin: *ejus testimonium*</note> is translated as "his witness of him" <note>Old English: *his cyðnisse his*</note> in both. In John 4:14, "a fountain of springing water" <note>Latin: *fons aquæ salientis*</note> is translated in both as "well of salt water" <note>Old English: *uælla uætres saltes*</note>, as if the translators had read the Latin word for "salty" <note>Latin: *salsi*</note> instead of "springing." In John 6:5, "had lifted up" <note>Latin: *sublevasset*</note> is translated in both as "under-heaved" <note>Old English: *underhof*</note>. In John 8:6, "downwards" <note>Latin: *deorsum*</note> is translated as "from apart" <note>Old English: *frü suunder*</note> in Lindisfarne and "separately" <note>Old English: *of syndrige*</note> in Rushworth, as if they had read the Latin for "separately" <note>Latin: *seorsum*</note>. In John 8:48, "do we not well say" <note>Latin: *nonne bene dicimus nos*</note> is translated in both as "did we not bless ourselves" <note>Old English: *ahne bloedsade ue usic*</note>. In John 10:10, "slaughters" <note>Latin: *mactat*</note> is translated as "eats" <note>Old English: *eteð*</note> in both. Finally, the error where "when/with" <note>Latin: *cùm*</note> is translated as "with" <note>Old English: *mið*</note>, which the specimen of the Rushworth gloss shown in the plate exhibits, will also be found in the Lindisfarne. <page-num>cv</page-num>

<header>### PREFACE <note>original Latin: "PROLEGOMENA"</note></header>

instances of this nature abound in the interlinear translations <note>glosses</note>, and their character and number make it impossible to believe that two independent translators would both arrive at the same strange or incorrect wording. One can rightly conclude, therefore, that alongside the standard Old English <note>Anglo-Saxon</note> version—which was based on a relatively accurate Latin text—there was another translation in circulation within the monastic communities. This version was likely based on a less reliable source and produced by men whose Latin was imperfect, intended to help less-educated monks understand the text.

However, having a shared origin does not mean the texts are identical. Differences in detail arose through repeated copying, with each scribe introducing their own variations and errors, adding supposed corrections to the original translation—which explains why we often see two or even three different English words offered for a single Latin phrase—and using the local dialect most familiar to the scribe. Thus, the Lindisfarne and Rushworth versions offer several points of difference. Owun’s translation in the Rushworth manuscript varies from the Lindisfarne manuscript in several ways:

1st. By the almost exclusive use of the letter *i* instead of *e*; for example, the prefix particles *ge-* and *be-* are almost always written as *gi-* and *bi-*, and the vowel combination <note>diphthong</note> *eo* is generally written as *io*.

2nd. The vowel combination *oe* (which represents the sounds *ē* or *ĕ*) is a marked characteristic of the Lindisfarne manuscript, but in the related Rushworth translation, it is changed into *eo* or *e*. While the scribe of the Bodley manuscript <note>The Rushworth Gospels, held in the Bodleian Library</note> does not reject it entirely, he uses it much less frequently.

3rd. The verb ending *-on* is generally changed by the Rushworth translator into *-un*, and in other cases, he shows a clear preference for the letter *u* over *o*.

4th. Regarding the use of a final *o* instead of an *e*, the instances in the Rushworth manuscript are far less common than those found in the Lindisfarne translation.

5th. The substitution of the letters *d*, *dt*, or *td* in place of *t*, which occurs frequently in the Lindisfarne manuscript, is only occasionally seen in the Rushworth manuscript by—

an occasional exchange of the letter *d* for *t*. 

6th. On the whole, the interlinear translation <note>gloss</note> of the Rushworth manuscript <note>referred to as "R."</note> adheres more closely to the correct grammatical endings <note>inflexional forms</note> of nouns and adjectives than the translation found in the Cotton manuscript. 

7th. Double and triple translations—where the scribe provides two or three English words for a single Latin one—are not as frequent in the Bodley manuscript <note>the Rushworth Gospels</note> as they are in the Cotton manuscript <note>the Lindisfarne Gospels</note>.

The Lindisfarne translator, Aldred—who clearly used an assistant to help translate the other three Gospels—wrote the entirety of the Gospel of Saint John with his own hand. This was the section which, according to his own notes, he "translated between the lines" <note>original: "overglossed"</note> specifically for his own benefit—that is, for the health of his soul. The translation of this fourth Gospel is notable for being written primarily in red ink and for its distinct spelling habits. However, its most striking features are the frequent use of runic symbols <note>term: rune; ancient Germanic alphabet characters used here as shorthand</note> and the presence of double translations¹. 

These alternative readings are mostly original and independent of the primary source material, making them very significant for study. They often provide rare words—such as in Mark 11:17, where the Rushworth manuscript offers both *cofa* <note>chamber</note> and *hydels* <note>hiding place</note>—or reflect the casual grammar of everyday speech. For instance, in John 10:28, the Lindisfarne text offers both "from my hands" <note>original: *of minum hondum*</note> and "from hand mine" <note>original: *of hond min*</note>. The first version follows a formal written source, while the latter reflects the common language of the people, much like the modern-day spoken Arabic of Syria and Egypt.

Its use was probably suggested by his master, Aldred. We find it twice in Saint Mark and more often (though still rarely) in Saint Luke. However, when Aldred himself takes up the pen, this rune becomes a regular feature, just as it is in the Durham Ritual <note>a 10th-century collection of prayers and rites</note>. All the specific stylistic habits of this second scribe become even more obvious from John 19:4 onward.

Two scribes, as we have seen, were also employed on the Rushworth translation <note>gloss</note>, which in the portion executed by Farman² <note>comprising the Gospel of Saint Matthew and the beginning of Saint Mark to chapter 2, verse 15</note> presents variations of a very marked character from the remainder of the version. 

**1st.** The portion translated by Farman is marked by the use of accent marks, which are entirely rejected by the second scribe. 

**2nd.** The handwriting and spelling <note>orthography</note> are unmistakably different from those employed in the other three Gospels, and reappear only once again, in John 18:1—3; this is sufficient proof that the two scribes were working during the same time period. 

**3rd.** The letter <term>thorn; the symbol þ, representing the "th" sound</term> is freely used in the Rushworth translation as far as Saint Mark 2:15, while in the rest of that translation, and throughout the translation of the Lindisfarne Gospels <note>referred to as "L."</note>, that character is completely excluded, except in the shorthand forms for "the" <note>þ</note> and "that" <note>þte</note>; the letter *k* is also freely used, *th* appears occasionally, and *q* appears twice (Matthew 2:1 and 25:39).

**North Anglian endings in *-es*.** **7th**, Nouns belonging to the first group of noun forms <note>specifically Rask's first declension, named after the pioneering Danish linguist Rasmus Rask</note> are given here in their correct forms. **8th**, "Disciples" <note>original Latin: *Discipuli*</note> is usually translated as "learners" <note>original Old English: *leorneras*</note>, a term not used in any other part of the Rushworth Gospels <note>referred to as "R."</note> or the Lindisfarne Gospels <note>referred to as "L."</note>. In this section also, and nowhere else in either of the two glosses, the word "behold" <note>original Latin: *ecce*</note> is translated as "look" or "behold" <note>original Old English: *sihðe*, literally "sight"</note>, a word used in the same sense by the translator of the Cotton Psalter <note>a famous 9th-century manuscript</note>.

The partial disregard for grammatical endings <note>inflexional forms</note> in these texts is attributed by some scholars to original regional differences <note>dialectic variation</note>, by others to the influence of foreign languages, and by others to the natural aging and simplification of the language. This loss of endings is probably caused at least as much by this natural decay as by the first two reasons. While it is highly probable that regional differences and foreign influence played some part in the results seen in our translations, unfortunately, there is not enough evidence to justify certain conclusions about how much they actually did. 

The adoption of the Old Norse verb form ending in *-a* <note>the infinitive</note>, the use of "the" <note>original: *ðe*</note> as the definite article, and the occasional appearance of a Scandinavian word do little to help us make exact statements about how much Old Norse mixed with the North Anglian dialect. Meanwhile, the few surviving traces of the Northumbrian dialect from before the Danish invasions—a few verses by the poet Cædmon, a few lines attributed to the monk Bede, and the carved Runic inscription on the Ruthwell Cross—are not enough to reconstruct the pure version of that ancient language. At one time, this speech was used from the River Humber to the Firth of Forth, and from the North Sea <note>original: "German Ocean"</note> to the Irish Channel, and was known as the:

<page-num>109 <note>original Roman numeral: cix</note></page-num>

<header># PREFACE <note>original Latin: "PROLEGOMENA"</note></header>

The period in which our interlinear translations <term>glosses: word-for-word translations written between the lines of a Latin text to help readers understand it</term> were created—that is, from the middle of the ninth to the last half of the tenth century—was a time of unparalleled chaos and suffering. This was the result of internal civil unrest <note>domestic anarchy</note> and invasions from abroad <note>referring to the Viking raids and settlements</note>. Under such a severe trial, the intellectual culture of even the best-organized societies could not remain unharmed; how much greater, then, would be the destruction brought by that time of trouble upon a poorly-organized state like Northumbria <note>an early medieval kingdom in northern England</note>. Amidst the collapse of their civilization, and the terrifying risks to life and property to which the unfortunate people were exposed, it is not surprising that the national language <note>Old English</note> would be affected. Just as the purity of a language depends on the education and study that come with national prosperity, its decay is caused by the neglect of learning <note>liberal study</note>, which is both a result and a sign of a nation’s suffering.

The interlinear translation of the *Lindisfarne Gospels* and also that of the *Durham Ritual*¹ were written in the area around Durham, and they accurately represent the dialect as it was spoken in that district during the tenth century. The *Rushworth translation* <note>the Rushworth gloss</note> takes us further south to the West-Riding of Yorkshire; meanwhile, the translation in the *Cotton Psalter*² (the oldest text of the four) probably shows the dialect of the country immediately south of the River Humber. In their general style of spelling <term>orthography</term> and in their grammatical forms—which are distinct from those of the West-Saxon dialect <note>the southern dialect of Old English associated with King Alfred the Great</note>—these remarkable texts agree with one another. A full listing of their similarities and differences would take up too much space here, but in the future, I hope to provide a detailed study alongside a full dictionary <note>glossary</note>.

<page-num>110 <note>original Roman numeral: cx</note></page-num>

...investigation of the dialects in which the four interlinear translations <term>glosses: word-for-word translations written between the lines of a Latin text</term> are written, based on the evidence they provide. These documents belong to a single period, after which, for several centuries, the literary history of Northumbria <note>referred to here as North Anglia</note> is a complete blank. We have no significant records of the language from the eleventh, twelfth, or thirteenth centuries¹; however, in the fourteenth century, numerous surviving works prove that the Northumbrian dialect had once again become a prominent literary language. Its poets from that era rivaled—and perhaps even surpassed—their southern contemporaries in both quantity and quality, right up to the time of famous writers like John Gower and Geoffrey Chaucer.

These interlinear translations were intended, as I have mentioned before, to make up for the poor understanding of Latin held by the clergy at that time. Just how poor that knowledge had become, and how completely learning had been neglected in the monasteries <note>cloister</note>, is clearly shown by the translations themselves. Both are full of what the scholar George Hickes calls "ignorant passages," where a word is left untranslated or a bizarre absurdity is written instead of the actual meaning. On specialized topics, such as the Latin names for animals and plants, the knowledge of our manuscript writers <note>scribes</note> is remarkably poor. For example, the plural form of a word as common as **sparrow** <note>original Latin: "passer"</note> is left without any translation²; and in the biblical passage, "**you are better than many sparrows**" <note>original Latin: "multis passeribus meliores estis"</note>, the Lindisfarne writer completely confuses the word for "sparrows" with the word for **sufferings** <note>original Latin: "passionibus"</note>.

<page-num>112 <note>original Roman numeral: cxii</note></page-num>

<header># PREFACE <note>original Latin: "PROLEGOMENA"</note></header>

West-Saxon, must surely have been unknown to scribes who invariably translate **fig tree** <note>original Latin: *ficus*</note> by **fig-beam** <note>original Old English: *ficbeam*; "beam" was the standard word for tree</note>, even going so far as gravely to tell the world that fig-trees are not to be gathered from hawthorn¹. Here the Rushworth gloss, if not faithful at least ingenious, offers **gorse and nuts**; our Yorkshire priest substituting for the unfamiliar Latin the wild growths of his north-country moor and woodland.

Geographical names are commonly either left blank or furnished with some general explanatory gloss. Thus for Asia, Dalmanutha, etc., we find **province or country** <note>original: *megð*</note>; Samaria is **nation** <note>original: *lioda*</note>; Samaritanus is rendered as **heathen man** <note>original: *hæðinmonn*</note>: names of towns, or any word mistaken for them, such as *probatica* <note>John 5:2; referring to the "sheep" gate or pool, but here mistaken for a place name</note>, are glossed **the city** <note>original: *ðæt byrig*</note>. In Matthew 2:18, Farman follows the West-Saxon version by giving the vernacular equivalent for the Hebrew word Rama <note>meaning "height"</note>; while his brother glossist, confounding it with the Latin word for branch <note>original: *ramus*</note>, has "a cry in the twigs²." Some medieval interpretation has probably suggested the gloss commonly used by our scribes for Galilee, **transmigration** <note>original: *geliornis*; Galilee was traditionally interpreted in the Middle Ages as meaning "passing over"</note>; and also the singular rendering for Iscariot, **memory of death** <note>original: *deaðes gemynd*; a literal translation of the Latin *mortis memoria*</note>. The glosses to proper names are worth notice; Peter is **rock or stone** <note>original: *carr ł stan*</note>; Alphaeus, **the white** <note>original: *ðæt huite*</note>; Pilate, **the reeve**³ <note>original: *se geroefa*</note>, etc. <margin>this Lazarus</margin> The marginal note at John 11:2, "this Lazarus

...talents he wisely leaves **talent** <note>original Latin: *talentum*</note> blank¹; and Matthew 10:29, **are not two sparrows sold for a penny?** <note>original Latin: *nonne duo passeres asse veneunt?*</note> he translates, "but two sparrows coming to him" (**coming to him** <note>original Latin: *ad se veniunt*</note>),—the Lindisfarne scribe varying the reading as follows, "do not two sparrows come out of one" (**from one** <note>original Latin: *a se*²</note>). The blunder here committed of treating the syllables of a word as independent vocables frequently occurs; and a really ingenious specimen of the kind will be found, Luke 24:29, where Owun <note>one of the scribes of the Rushworth Gospels</note> gets the sentence, "Evening draweth nigh, thou knowest³," out of **it draws toward evening** <note>original Latin: *advesperascit*</note>, by splitting up the word and glossing its last syllable as part of **to know** <note>original Latin: *scire*</note>.

Still, in spite of this list of errors, which might be indefinitely extended, it is only just to our glossists <note>scribes who wrote translations between the lines of a Latin text</note> to add that where they failed it was for want of Latin, not from lack of painstaking; their anxiety to give every particle in the text its vernacular equivalent is attested by the abundance and variety of compound words in the versions; and whenever they were dissatisfied with the first gloss of a word, a second, third, or even fourth display their zeal; sometimes, it is true, after a fashion suggesting that too much of that quality is dangerous when combined with too little learning, as Luke 6:22, where the Lindisfarne scribe, determined to be right somehow, boldly renders **evil** <note>original Latin: *malum*</note>, **evil or apple-tree** <note>original Old English: *yfel ł apoltré*</note> = evil or apple-tree! <note>The scribe confused the Latin *mālum* (apple) with *malum* (evil).</note>

often grossly misrepresenting the Latin text, sacrifice their native speech patterns in their anxiety to render with strict literalism every word of that text; compared with this object, elegance and even clarity of expression in their native tongue were deemed of no moment. Thus, John 1:27, **"I am not worthy that I undo"** (Rushworth)^1 <note>original: *ne am ic wyrðe þ undoe R.*</note>; in slavish imitation of the Latin, the pronoun is omitted before **undo** <note>original: *undoe*</note>. Faults of this nature, defect or superfluity of pronouns, will be found in abundance. Both glossists <note>translators who wrote English words between the lines of a Latin manuscript</note> constantly render the Latin deponent verb <note>a verb that is passive in form but active in meaning</note> by a passive participle—**"having followed"** <note>original Latin: *assecuto*</note>, **"followed"** (Lindisfarne) <note>original: *gefylgde L.*</note>, **"followed"** (Rushworth) <note>original: *offylligde R.*</note>, Luke 1:3; **"they will persecute"** <note>original Latin: *persequentur*</note>, **"they are persecuted"** (Lindisfarne) <note>original: *oehtad biðon L.*</note>, Luke 11:49^2. The combination of a verb and participle in Latin is usually represented by two verbs without the joining word "and"—**"rising he went away"** <note>original Latin: *exsurgens abiit*</note>, **"arose went"** (Lindisfarne) <note>original: *aras foerde L.*</note>, **"arose went"** (Rushworth) <note>original: *aras eode R.*</note>, Luke 1:39^3; **"and responding his mother said"** <note>original Latin: *et respondens mater ejus dixit*</note>, **"and answered mother his said"** (Lindisfarne and Rushworth) <note>original: *⁊ geonduearde moder his cuoeð L. R.*</note>, Luke 1:60. The glossists especially violate the natural flow of their language by the way in which they translate the ablative absolute <note>a Latin grammatical construction indicating circumstances, like "the sun having set"</note>—**"while they were ascending"** <note>original Latin: *ascendentibus illis*</note>, **"by those ascending"**^4 (Lindisfarne and Rushworth) <note>original: *stigendum ðæm L. R.*</note>, Luke 2:42; **"and with the ships drawn up to land, having left all things"** <note>original Latin: *et subductis ad terram navibus, relictis omnibus*</note>, **"and were led-under to earth ships, left all"** (Lindisfarne)^5 <note>original: *⁊ woeron underlædet to eorðo scioppo, forletno allum L.*</note>, Luke 5:11; **"while he was speaking"** <note>original Latin: *illo loquente*</note>, **"him speaking"** (Lindisfarne and Rushworth) <note>original: *hine sprecende L. R.*</note>, Luke 8:49, here the use of **him** <note>original: *hine*</note> as a dative is to be noted. The indirect construction <note>original Latin: *structio obliqua*; a grammatical structure where a statement is reported rather than quoted directly</note> is often clumsy and unidiomatic—**"it is easier, however, for heaven and earth to pass away,"** **"easier it is truly heaven and the earth that they pass away"** <note>original: *eaðor is uūt heofon ⁊ þ eorðo ꝥte fgeleore*</note> (Lindisfarne Gospels)¹, Luke 16:17; **"we do not want this man to reign [over us],"** **"we do not want this one that he should reign"** <note>original: *nallo we ðiosne ꝥte gerixage*</note>² (Lindisfarne and Rushworth Gospels), Luke 19:14; **"they are certain that John is a prophet,"** **"unwavering they are concerning John the prophet that he were"** <note>original: *untuendlic sindon frõ Ioħ witga ꝥte woere*</note>³ (Lindisfarne and Rushworth Gospels), Luke 20:6. These may serve as examples of the departure from general grammatical usage everywhere prevalent in these texts, and mainly to be set down to a spirit of servile literalism <term>servile literalism: an overly-strict translation style that follows the source language's word order so closely that the result sounds unnatural in the target language</term> which has also prompted glosses <note>words written between the lines of a manuscript to explain the text</note> actually subverting the sense of a passage by the attempt to give an exact verbal rendering, such as **"permit,"** **"sending through"** <note>original: *ðerhsende*—the translator likely confused the Latin *per-* (through) and *mitte* (send), though the word actually means "allow"</note>⁴ (Lindisfarne), Matthew 8:21; **"having been drawn up [to shore],"** **"led under"** <note>original: *underlædet*—the translator misinterpreted the Latin *sub-* (up/away) as "under" and *ductis* as "led"</note>⁵ (Lindisfarne), Luke 5:11; **"executioner,"** **"observer"** <note>original: *sceawere*—the Latin *speculator* can mean a scout or guard, but here refers to an executioner; the translator chose a literal meaning of "one who looks"</note>⁶ (Lindisfarne and Rushworth), Mark 6:27. Nevertheless, every deduction being made for the shortcomings of our two glossists, they are entitled to the gratitude of all who study the old Teutonic <note>Germanic</note> speech of the English people; to their labours we owe the largest and most consistent specimens of that language as it was spoken throughout the north of England. These glosses of the Gospels, if compared with that of the *Ritual* <note>The Durham Ritual, another Northumbrian manuscript</note>, will prove to have been written with superior care and correctness; if with the *Cotton Psalter*, the comparison will show their language to be more thoroughly and consistently North Anglian than the rendering of the Psalms.

# PECULIARITIES OF ORTHOGRAPHY. <note>Orthography refers to the conventional spelling system of a language. This section analyzes how Northumbrian scribes spelled words differently than the more common West-Saxon standard.</note>

I. VOWELS. Northumbrian *a* <note>The Northumbrian dialect was spoken in Northern England and differs significantly from the West-Saxon dialect used in the south.</note> for West-Saxon *e*,—*shackle* <note>original: *fatter*; West-Saxon: *fetor*</note> in the Gospel of Mark, chapter 5, verse 4; *riches* <note>original: *walana*</note> in Matthew, chapter 13, verse 22. Especially in the present participle,—*rejoicing* <note>original: *gefeande* in the Lindisfarne Gospels (L.) and *gifeande* in the Rushworth Gospels (R.)</note> in Luke, chapter 22, verse 5; *praising* and *blessing* <note>original: *lofando* and *gebloedsando* in the Lindisfarne Gospels (L.)</note> in Luke, chapter 24, verse 53. In nouns identifying a person by their action (agent nouns) usually ending in *ere*, *a* is often the second-to-last vowel.

Northumbrian *æ* for West-Saxon *ea*,—*all* <note>original: *all* = *eall*</note>, *old* <note>original: *ald* = *eald*</note> and its derivatives, *arm* <note>original: *arm* = *earm* (referring to the limb)</note>, and *wretched* <note>original: *arm* = *earm* (referring to a miserable person)</note> are the regular forms in both glosses <note>A "gloss" is an interlinear translation or explanation written between the lines of a text</note>, with the exception of the last example, which is generally written as *eorm* <note>original: *eorm*</note> in the Rushworth Gospels (R.).

Northumbrian *æ* for West-Saxon *ea*, *e*,—*also* <note>original: *æc* = *eac*, *ec*</note> in both Lindisfarne and Rushworth, Mark, chapter 8, verses 28, 29; *night* <note>original: *næht* = *neaht*</note> in Luke, chapter 12, verse 20; *easily* <note>original: *æðe* in Rushworth = *eaðe* in Lindisfarne</note> in John, chapter 8, verse 19; *few* <note>original: *fæs* in Lindisfarne = *feas* in Rushworth</note> in Luke, chapter 15, verse 12; *yea* <note>original: *gæ* = *ge*</note> in Matthew, chapter 11, verse 9.

Northumbrian *e* for West-Saxon *æ*,—*to readers* <note>original: *redendum* = *rædendum*</note> in the Introduction to John, page 1, line 11. This form prevails in both glosses in the words *where* <note>original: *hwer*</note>, *there* <note>original: *ðer*</note>, *were* <note>original: *were*, *weron*</note>, *said* <note>original: *cweð*, *cwedon*</note>. *e* for West-Saxon *eo*,—*light* <note>original: *leht*</note> in Luke, chapter 11, verse 33; *money* <note>original: *feh*</note> in Luke, chapter 22, verse 5. This substitution is regular in both glosses. *e* for West-Saxon *o*,—*or* <note>original: *eðða* in Rushworth = *oððæ* in Lindisfarne</note> in Matthew, chapter 5, verse 17; *oxen* <note>original: *exin*, *exen* = *oxen*</note> in John, chapter 2, verse 15.

Northumbrian *ea* for West-Saxon *æ*,—*sinner* <note>original: *bearswinig* in Rushworth = *bærsynig* in Lindisfarne</note> in Luke, chapter 3, verse 12. *ea*, *eo* for West-Saxon *e*,—*to bear* <note>original: *beara* = *beranne*</note> in Matthew, chapter 3, verse 11; *they bear* <note>original: *beorað* = *berað*</note> in John, chapter 21, verse 10.

Northumbrian *i* for West-Saxon *e*,—*desiring* <note>original: *giornende*, *giornde*</note> in Luke, chapter 18, verse 35; *yesterday* <note>original: *gioster-doeg*</note> in John, chapter 4, verse 52; *I am* <note>original: *biom* = *beom*</note>, *leprosy* <note>original: *hriofol* = *hreafol*</note>; for examples of the ending *i* instead of *e*, see John, chapter 21, verses 9, 22, 25 in the Lindisfarne Gospels. The prefix *gi-* <note>original: *gi-*</note>, which is the usual spelling for the formative particle in the Rushworth Gospels, rarely occurs in the Lindisfarne Gospels until John, chapter 20, verse 23, after which it becomes the regular form throughout the end of the Gospel and the appended entry. Itacism <note>Itacism is a linguistic phenomenon where different vowels or diphthongs evolve to be pronounced like the letter "i" (ee sound).</note> is a striking peculiarity of the Rushworth gloss.

Northumbrian *io* for West-Saxon *i*,—*he leaned* <note>original: *gelionade*, *gehlionade*</note> in Mark, chapter 2, verse 15; *womb* <note>original: *ionnaðe*</note> in Luke, chapter 1, verse 31. This substitution only takes place when
