the vowel is short. In the Lindisfarne Gospels, John chapter 5, verse 6, *then* <note>original: *ðionne*</note> appears for *then* <note>original: *ðonne*</note>, which is a remarkable instance of an *i* being inserted into this form of the pronoun.

Northumbrian *oe* or *oæ* used for West-Saxon *e* or *æ*. This form is very prominent in both glosses <note>An interlinear translation where Old English words are written above the Latin text</note>, and it especially prevails in the Lindisfarne Gospels (L.); the scribe of the Rushworth Gospels (R.) often uses *eo* or, rarely, *oi* in its place—such as *persecuting* <note>original: *oihtande*</note> in Rushworth, Matthew chapter 5, verse 43. This diphthong <note>A sound formed by the combination of two vowels in a single syllable</note> *oe* is used regardless of whether the vowel it replaces was originally long or short. We find the forms for *we* <note>original: *woe*</note>, *where* <note>original: *hwoer*</note>, *everyone* <note>original: *eghwoelc*</note>, *self* <note>original: *soelf*</note>, *twelve* <note>original: *twoelf*</note>, and *well* <note>original: *woel*</note>, where the West-Saxon *e* is certainly short.

Both glosses are further marked by a redundancy and doubling of vowels—*goes* <note>original: *gaas*</note> in Lindisfarne, Mark chapter 16, verse 15; *go* <note>original: *gaað*</note> in Lindisfarne, and *goes* <note>original: *gaas*</note> in Rushworth, Mark chapter 14, verse 13; *Spirit* <note>original: *gaast*</note> in Lindisfarne, Mark chapter 1, verse 8; *you see* <note>original: *gesiist*</note> in Lindisfarne, Luke chapter 6, verse 41. We also see *good* <note>original: *goodne*</note>, *especially* <note>original: *sunndorlice*</note>, *Savior* <note>original: *hæelend*</note>, *produce* <note>original: *gestrionaige*</note>, *received* <note>original: *onfeing*</note>, *wept* <note>original: *woeap*</note>, *do* <note>original: *doað*</note>, *receive* <note>original: *onfoiæ*</note>, and *eight* <note>original: *eahtowe*</note>. This double vowel often takes the place of a written accent mark—for example, in John chapter 3, verse 25, Lindisfarne uses *judgment* <note>original: *dóm*</note> while Rushworth uses *judgment* <note>original: *doom*</note>.

## II. CONSONANTS.

Northumbrian *c* used for West-Saxon *g*,—*finger* <note>original: *fincer*</note> in Rushworth is the same as *finger* <note>original: *finger*</note> in Lindisfarne, John chapter 20, verse 27; *backwards* <note>original: *bæclinc*</note> for *backwards* <note>original: *bæcling*</note> in Rushworth, Mark chapter 8, verse 33.

Northumbrian *ch* used for West-Saxon *c*,—*use* <note>original: *gibruche*</note> for *use* <note>original: *gibruce*</note> in Rushworth, John chapter 6, verse 5; *works* <note>original: *werches*</note> for *works* <note>original: *werces*</note> in Rushworth, Mark chapter 5, verse 14; the forms *people* and *of the people* <note>original: *folche*, *folches*</note> are the regular forms in Rushworth; *much* <note>original: *michel*</note> in Lindisfarne, Mark chapter 4, verse 5; and *me* <note>original: *mech*</note> in Lindisfarne, John chapter 6, verse 35.

Northumbrian *ch* used for West-Saxon *h*,—*bought* <note>original: *bochton*</note> in Lindisfarne is the same as *bought* <note>original: *bohton*</note> in Rushworth, John chapter 4, verse 8; *whatever* <note>original: *suæchuæt*</note> for *whatever* <note>original: *suæhuæt*</note> in Lindisfarne, Matthew chapter 18, verses 18 and 19; *though* <note>original: *ðæch*</note> in Lindisfarne for *though* <note>original: *ðeh*</note> in Rushworth, John chapter 4, verse 2.

Northumbrian *d* used for West-Saxon *ð* <note>The letter "eth," pronounced like the "th" in "the."</note>,—*heathens* <note>original: *hædno*</note> in Lindisfarne, Mark chapter 13, verse 10; *crowed* <note>original: *cræd*</note> in Rushworth, Matthew chapter 26, verse 34. Conversely, *ð* is used for West-Saxon *d*,—*words* <note>original: *worðo*</note> in Rushworth, John chapter 15, verse 14; *inward* <note>original: *innwearð*</note> in Lindisfarne is the same as *inward* <note>original: *ionaword*</note> in Rushworth, Mark chapter 7, verse 23. Both of these changes occur frequently in the Lindisfarne Gospels.

Northumbrian *d* or *td* used for West-Saxon *t*; this is found chiefly in the gloss of Lindisfarne, where *what* <note>original: *huæd* or *huætd*</note> is commonly substituted for *what* <note>original: *hwæt*</note>, and also *crowd* <note>original: *ðread*</note> for *crowd* <note>original: *ðreat*</note>, unless it is followed by a vowel, in which case the *t* usually reappears in this word. The letter *ð* is used for West-Saxon *w* in the word *four-footed* <note>original: *feoðorfota*</note> for *four-footed* <note>original: *feoworfota*</note> in both Lindisfarne and Rushworth, John chapter 4, verse 12.

Northumbrian *g* used for West-Saxon *c*,—*cold* <note>original: *galdes*</note> for *cold* <note>original: *caldes*</note> in Rushworth, Matthew chapter 10, verse 42; *I said* <note>original: *sægdig*</note> for *I said* <note>original: *sægde ic*</note> in Lindisfarne, Matthew chapter 16, verse 11; *I shall repay* <note>original: *forgeldig*</note> for *I shall repay* <note>original: *forgelda ic*</note> in Lindisfarne, Matthew chapter 18, verse 26; *drunk* <note>original: *indrungno*</note> for *drunk* <note>original: *indruncno*</note> in Lindisfarne, John chapter 2, verse 10. Also *g* for West-Saxon *h*,—*saw* <note>original: *gesæg*</note> in Rushworth for *saw* <note>original: *gesæh*</note> in Lindisfarne, Matthew chapter 3, verse 16. Finally, *g* for West-Saxon *w*,—*trusted* <note>original: *trugude* in Lindisfarne, *gitrygade* in Rushworth</note> for *trusted* <note>original: *getruwade*</note>, John chapter 2, verse 24; *thrice* <note>original: *ðriga*</note> for *thrice* <note>original: *ðriowa*</note> in Rushworth, Matthew chapter 26, verse 34; *follow* <note>original: *fulguia*</note> for *follow* <note>original: *fulvia*</note> in Lindisfarne, John chapter i. 26.

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of Northumbrian Old English orthography, shifting from the use of vowels and diphthongs to the specific ways consonants—particularly g, h, r, t, and w—were written and pronounced in Northern dialects compared to the West-Saxon standard.</meta>

### PECULIARITIES OF ORTHOGRAPHY.

Northumbrian <note>N.</note> uses *gh* or *hg* where West-Saxon <note>W. S.</note> uses *h* or *g*—*afterwards* <note>original: *sighðana* = *sihðana*</note> in the Ritual of Durham <note>Arg. J.</note>, page 2, line 2; *any* <note>original: *ænight*</note> in the Lindisfarne Gospels <note>L.</note> = *any* <note>original: *ænig*</note> in the Rushworth Gospels <note>R.</note>, John chapter 5, verse 30; *desert* <note>original: *woestihg*</note> in L. = *desert* <note>original: *woestig*</note> in R., Matthew chapter 14, verse 15. The letter *g* is sometimes omitted—*unwashed* <note>original: *unðuenum*</note> in L. = *unwashed* <note>original: *unðwegenum*</note> in R., Matthew chapter 15, verse 20; *called* <note>original: *cede*</note> in R. = *called* <note>original: *ceigde*</note> in L., Luke chapter 14, verse 16. The root *g* is occasionally softened into an *i* sound in the portion of the Rushworth gloss translated by the scribe Farman—*rod* or *staff* <note>original: *ierd* = *gerd*</note>, Matthew chapter 10, verse 10; *yoke* <note>original: *ioc* = *geoc*</note>, chapter 11, verses 29 and 30; *yes* <note>original: *ia* = *gee*</note>, chapter 13, verse 51.

Northumbrian uses *h* where West-Saxon uses *c*—*secretly* <note>original: *deglihe*</note> in L. = *secretly* <note>original: *degullice*</note> in R., Matthew chapter 24, verse 3; *great* <note>original: *mihil*</note> in L. = *great* <note>original: *micel*</note> in R., Matthew chapter 4, verse 16. The aspirate <note>the 'h' sound</note> is abundantly employed at the beginning of words where in West-Saxon it is not allowed—*oaths* <note>original: *haðas*</note> in R. = *oaths* <note>original: *aðas*</note> in L., Matthew chapter 5, verse 33; *leaders* or *centurions* <note>original: *haldormenn*</note> in L., Matthew chapter 8, verse 13; *of the living* <note>original: *hlifgiendra*</note> in L. = *of the living* <note>original: *lifgendra*</note> in R., Matthew chapter 22, verse 32. Instances where the initial aspirate is left out occur, but less frequently—*seventy* <note>original: *unseofuntig* = *hundseofuntig*</note> in Jerome’s Epistles <note>Hier. Ep.</note>; *of the master of the house* <note>original: *feder-iorodes*</note> in L., Matthew chapter 13, verse 52.

In many words, the letter *r* is frequently inserted into the root—*evening* <note>original: *efern*</note> in L. = *evening* <note>original: *efen*</note> in R., Matthew chapter 14, verse 15; *wilderness* <note>original: *woestern*</note> in R. = *wilderness* <note>original: *woesten*</note> in L., Luke chapter 15, verse 4. This form is most noticeable in the verbs *left/permitted* <note>original: *forleorta*</note> and *feared/dreaded* <note>original: *ondrearda*</note>, which correspond to the West-Saxon *forletan* and *ondredan*. The letter is occasionally doubled—*your* <note>original: *iurra*</note> in L. = *your* <note>original: *eower*</note> in R.; *your* <note>original: *iurrne*</note> in L. = *your* <note>original: *eowrum*</note> in R., Matthew chapter 5, verse 16.

Northumbrian uses *t* for West-Saxon *d*—*sent* <note>original: *asendet*</note> in L., John chapter 9, verse 7; *head* <note>original: *heafot*</note> in L., Luke chapter 23, verse 33. Remarkable instances occur of the change from *ð* <note>the 'th' sound</note> to *t* in the pronoun *you* <note>original: *ðu*</note> when it is attached to the end of a verb—*you see* <note>original: *gesiistu*</note> in L. and R., Matthew chapter 7, verse 3; *what do you weep for? whom do you seek?* <note>original: *huæd uoepestu huelc soecas ðu*</note> in L., and *what do you weep for? whom do you seek?* <note>original: *hwæt woepastu hwelcne soecestu*</note> in R., John chapter 20, verse 15.

The letter *w* is occasionally added to a word starting with a vowel—*outside* <note>original: *wuteard*</note> in L. = *outside* <note>original: *utaword*</note> in R., Luke chapter 11, verse 40; *let us* <note>original: *wutun*</note> is the regular Northumbrian form for the West-Saxon *utan*. It is also added to a vowel preceded by *s*—*sinner* <note>original: *bearswinig*</note> in R. = *sinner* <note>original: *bærsynig*</note> in L., Luke chapter 3, verse 12; *separate/individual* <note>original: *suindrige*</note> in L. = *separate* <note>original: *syndrigne*</note> in R., Mark chapter 8, verse 2. In the gloss of Lindisfarne, the *u* used for the *w* sound is often omitted—*wash* <note>original: *aðoa*</note> in Luke chapter 7, verse 37; *said* <note>original: *coeð*</note> = *said* <note>original: *cweþ*</note> in R., Matthew chapter 8, verse 19; *four* <note>original: *feor* = *feower*</note>, *queen* <note>original: *coen* = *cuoen*</note>, *sister* <note>original: *soester* = *suoester*</note>.

# PECULIARITIES OF INFLEXION.

## I. SUBSTANTIVES. 
Throughout the gloss of the Lindisfarne Gospels <note>L.</note>, and that of the latter three Gospels in the Rushworth manuscript <note>R.</note>, the endings of the first declension <note>A system of word groupings used by the scholar Erasmus Rask</note> do not appear; they are, however, quite numerous in the portion of the Rushworth gloss translated by the scribe Farman. The following are the forms usually substituted: 

**Singular:**
*   **Nominative/Accusative:** star <note>original: *steorra*</note>
*   **Genitive:** star's <note>original: *steorres*, *steorra*</note>
*   **Dative:** [to/for a] star <note>original: *steorre*</note>

**Plural:**
*   **Nominative/Accusative (masculine):** stars <note>original: *steorres*, *steorra*</note>
*   **Nominative/Accusative (neuter):** stars <note>original: *steorro*</note>
*   **Genitive:** of stars <note>original: *steorra*, *steorrana*</note>

But these forms are not strictly followed; we find the nominative singular earth <note>original: *eorðo*, *-u*</note> and the genitive/dative earth <note>original: *eorðu*, *-e*</note>. A dative singular ending in *-um* occurs in Rushworth, Luke chapter 3, verse 4: books <note>original: *boecum*; Latin: *libris*</note>. 

In the first class of Rask’s second declension, the nominative and accusative plural often end in *a*, *e*, or *o*, such as words <note>original: *worda*, *-e*</note> and signs <note>original: *taceno*</note>. This irregularity is more frequent in the Lindisfarne gloss. The nominative plural masculine of this group sometimes ends in *-es*—stones <note>original: *stanes*</note> or loaves <note>original: *hlafes*</note> in Rushworth, Matthew chapter 4, verse 3. 

The genitive plural of this class of nouns, as well as those of the first two classes of Rask’s third declension, substitutes *-ana* or *-ona* for the standard *-a*—of days <note>original: *dagana*, *dagona*; Latin: *dierum*</note> and of trees <note>original: *treuana*, *treona*; Latin: *arborum*</note>. 

Feminine nouns of Rask’s second declension often take a final *e*, such as time <note>original: *tide*</note> or righteousness <note>original: *soðfæstnisse*</note>, and they form the genitive singular in *-es* and the nominative and accusative plural in *-as*—blasphemies <note>original: *efolsungas*; Latin: *blasphemiæ*</note> and thoughts <note>original: *smeaungas*; Latin: *cogitationes*</note>. 

Our texts often show inconsistencies in the forms and genders of nouns; for example, we find different forms for bridegroom <note>original: *brydgum*, *brydguma*</note> and the plural for temptations <note>original: *costunges*, *costungo*</note>. We also see shifting gender markers like the woman <note>original: *þ wif*, *ðio wif*</note>, the word <note>original: *þ word*, *ðone word*</note>, and the maiden <note>original: *þ mægden*, *ðære mægdene*</note>. Other examples include spirits <note>original: *gastas*, *gasto*</note> and dens <note>original: *holas* in Lindisfarne, *holo* in Rushworth; Latin: *foveas*</note>. 

Forms where the only difference is the final letter (*a*, *e*, or *o*) can hardly be considered essential variations in such a fluid state of the language as these glosses show. They are often found together in the same verse. The only logical conclusion is that the pronunciation of these final letters was so blurred that the scribes did not feel it necessary to distinguish between them in writing. [...diverging] from those found in West-Saxon <note>The dominant literary dialect of Old English used in the south</note>; for example, feet <note>original: *fotum*</note> and one <note>original: *anum*</note> in the accusative singular; stones <note>original: *stæner*</note> in the nominative plural, and lambs <note>original: *lombor*</note> in the accusative plural—these two bear a striking resemblance to Old Norse. Also found is the nominative plural form for table-guests <note>original: *efenmetti*</note> in the Lindisfarne <note>L.</note> Gospel of Matthew (26:26), perhaps in imitation of the corresponding Latin word *cœnati* <note>meaning 'those who have dined'</note>; and fathers or elders <note>original: *fædrum* ɫ *ældrum*; the symbol ɫ means 'or'</note> in the nominative plural in the Rushworth <note>R.</note> Gospel of John (6:31). We also see various forms for the genitive plural: of teeth <note>original: *toðana*</note>, of teachers <note>original: *larwara*</note>, of travelers <note>original: *wegara*</note>, of ways <note>original: *wegas*</note>, and of heavens <note>original: *heofnas*</note>. This last form, occasionally found in West-Saxon poetry, occurs several times in the Rushworth manuscript, to which it is peculiar. A very rare form of concrete noun is also found in Rushworth—divorce <note>original: *forletnisse*</note>, corresponding to the Latin *dimissa* <note>meaning 'a woman sent away'</note> in Matthew 19:9.

## II. **Adjectives.** 
Consistently with what has been observed regarding nouns of Rask's first declension <note>A system of word classification by the scholar Erasmus Rask</note>, the corresponding form of the adjective—the definite <note>The 'weak' form, used typically after words like 'the' or 'this'</note>—is missing in these glosses, except, as might be expected, in the Rushworth version of St. Matthew. In the indefinite <note>The 'strong' form, used when no article is present</note>, however, the form of the West-Saxon dialect is generally followed, but alongside it several anomalies occur. Instead of the ending *-um* for the dative singular masculine and neuter, *-e* is frequently used. For the feminine genitive and dative singular, which usually end in *-re*, two forms ending in *-ere* and *-er* are often found, such as great <note>original: *miclere*, *-er*</note>; this second form also appears in Old High German. For the masculine singular accusative ending in *-ne*, *-e* or *-a* are frequently written. The highly unusual ending *-um* used for the nominative and accusative cases of nouns is sometimes, though very rarely, used for adjectives—any good <note>original: *ænigum good*</note> in Rushworth, Mark 10:18.

## III. **Pronouns.** 
The word for "I" <note>original: *Ic*</note> is rarely written as *ih* (Rushworth, Luke 14:18). In the dative and accusative singular of "I" and "you" <note>original: *ic* and *ðu*</note>, the forms *mec*, *mech*, *meh* <note>me</note> and *ðec*, *ðech*, *ðeh* <note>you</note> are in general use. The dual forms <note>special pronouns used only when referring to exactly two people, such as 'we two'</note> of these pronouns occur only in the Rushworth gloss of St. Matthew. The forms for the dative and accusative plural commonly employed are *usic*, *usig*, *usih* <note>us</note> and *iow*, *iowih*, *iuih*, *iwih*, *iuch* <note>you all</note>. Their possessive forms <note>our and your</note> are *urer*, *usser* and *iower*, *iuer*. In the third person, the feminine singular forms *hia*, *sio*, *ðio*, and *ðiu* <note>she/her</note> are in common use; in the genitive and dative singular form *ðære* <note>of/to her</note>, the ending *-e* is often omitted. The form *hia* <note>they/them</note> frequently occurs as the nominative and accusative plural. The word *ðisse* or *ðissa* is often used instead of *ðisum* <note>this/these</note>; and *huodhuoegu* (Lindisfarne) or *hwætwoegno* (Rushworth, John 7:4) is used for "something" <note>original: *hwætwegu*</note>. ->cxxiv<-
->PECULIARITIES OF INFLEXION.<-

...offer several changes from the West-Saxon <note>The standard literary dialect of southern England</note>; for example: **third** <note>original: *ðirdda* = *ðridda*</note>, **seven** <note>original: *seofo* = *seofon*</note>, **eight** <note>original: *æhtowe* = *eahta*; this form is unique to the Rushworth manuscript</note>, **ten** <note>original: *tea* = *tyn*</note> in the Lindisfarne <note>L.</note> and Rushworth <note>R.</note> manuscripts, Luke 17:12; **eleven** <note>original: *ællefno*</note> in L., **eleventh** <note>original: *enleftan*</note> in R., Matthew 28:16; **fifteenth** <note>original: *fifzegða*</note> in R., Luke 3:1; **thirty** <note>original: *ðrittih*</note> in L., John 5:5; **sixty** <note>original: *sexdeih*</note> in L., Matthew 13:8.

IV. These texts offer many anomalies of inflexion <note>The way word endings change to express grammatical categories like tense or person</note> in the verb. Throughout the whole of L. and generally in R. (excepting the Gospel of St. Matthew), the final ***n*** is dropped from the infinitive <note>The "to" form of a verb, like "to speak"</note>; and while the final ***a*** is prevalent, it is by no means the only ending found. Final ***e*** and ***æ*** are common in this mood; the final ***o*** also appears—**to say** <note>original: *sægcō* in L., *sæcgō* in R., John 16:25</note>. The form **to heal** <note>original: *Hælon* instead of *hælan*</note> occurs in R., Matthew 12:10; **to reap** <note>original: *girip* in R., corresponding to *gehrioppa* in L., John 4:38</note> presents an instance of the infinitive without the usual formative suffix. In the 1st person indicative present (the "I" form), endings in ***o*** and ***u*** are common; three verbs take the ending ***m***, namely: **I see** <note>original: *geseom*, *-am*, *-ium*, *-iom*</note>; **I do** <note>original: *doam*, *dom*, *doom*</note>; and **I am** <note>original: *beom*, *bium*</note>; (**you are** <note>original: *bist*</note> is the 2nd person singular form in L. and R., Luke 22:32.) This same termination of the 1st person singular present is found in Old High German <note>An early form of the German language</note> in verbs whose characteristic vowel is ***ō*** or ***ē***—**I anoint** <note>original: *salbōm*</note> and **I have** <note>original: *habēm*</note>. In the verbal termination ***-iga***, the ***i*** is often changed into ***a***—**I tempt** <note>original: *costaga*</note>, **I perish** <note>original: *losaga*</note>, **I die** <note>original: *deadaga*</note>, instead of *costiga*, *losiga*, *deadiga*; this form is frequent in L., where we also find another ending in ***-aiga*** which does not occur in R.—**you congratulate/rejoice with [me]** <note>original: *efnegeðoncaiges* in L., corresponding to *efnegeðoncigas* in R., Luke 15:6</note>. For the personal termination ***-iað*** used in West-Saxon, ***-að*** is often employed in these glosses <note>Interlinear translations added between the lines of the original Latin text</note>.

The personal terminations ***að*** and ***st*** are changed into ***-es***; this form, which is almost universal in the gloss of L. and in the last three Gospels of R., is not so closely followed in Farman's version of St. Matthew <note>Farman was one of the primary scribes/translators of the Rushworth Gospels</note>; the ending ***eð*** is not entirely rejected—**watches** <note>original: *wæceð* in R., Matthew 25:13</note>; **believes** <note>original: *gelefeð* in L., John 1:50</note>. Likewise, the 3rd person singular ***-es*** is sometimes changed into ***-et***—**destroys** <note>original: *spillet* in R., Luke 17:33</note>; **falls** <note>original: *fallet* in R., Luke 11:17</note>. In the gloss of R., two examples occur of the change of ***-es*** into ***-en***—**they fast** <note>original: *fæsten* in the 2nd and 3rd person present plural, Matthew 6:16 and 9:15</note>.

The terminations ***s*** and ***on*** are sometimes lost—**[he] calls you** <note>original: *ceiga* ðec, translating the Latin *vocat te*, Mark 10:49</note>; **[he] sent two** <note>original: *sende twoege* in R., Mark 14:13</note>; **[he/it] covers** <note>original: *awria* in L., Luke 8:16</note>; **[they] answered** <note>original: *ondsworade* in the 3rd person plural, R., John 10:33</note>.

Very often in the gloss of L., occasionally in that of R.,

->cxxv<-
->PECULIARITIES OF INFLEXION.<-

Verbs that usually have a "closed" past tense <note>Strong verbs that change their internal vowel, like "sing/sang"</note> in the common language sometimes take an "open" past tense <note>Weak verbs that add a suffix like -ed, like "walk/walked"</note>—**he slept** <note>original: *slepde* in L., Luke 8:23</note>; **grasped** <note>original: *gegrippde* in L., *gigrap* in R., Luke 9:39</note>; so also **asked** <note>original: *gefraignade* and a shortened form *gefraign*</note>, **touched** <note>original: *gehrinade*</note>, and **they ascended** <note>original: *astagdon*</note>.

The third-person plural of the past tense <note>The "they" form of completed actions</note> occasionally shows the ending ***-es***—**they showed** or **proclaimed** <note>original: *æwades* or *mersades*, equivalent to *æwadon* or *mersadon* in L., Mark 3:12</note>—a feature unique to that specific translation.

The first and third-person singular past tense <note>The "I" and "he/she" forms</note> often end in ***-un*** or ***-on***—**I went forth** <note>original: *ic foerdun*, translating the Latin *processi* in R., John 8:42</note>; **he said** <note>original: *cuedon*, translating the Latin *dixit* in L., Matthew 16:12</note>.

The loss of the consonant at the end of plural present tense verbs, which was happening in the West-Saxon dialect <note>The standard literary language of southern England</note>, is occasionally extended to the plural past tense—**you thought again** <note>original: *eftðohto gie* in L., Mark 8:18</note>; **you took** <note>original: *nomo gie* in L., Matthew 26:55</note>.

In these combinations of a verb and a pronoun, the vowel that remains after the final ***n*** is dropped in the present tense is kept, and the pronoun is attached directly to the end of the verb—**honour you** <note>original: *arogie*</note>, **know you** <note>original: *wutugie*</note>, **can you** <note>original: *magogie*</note>, **learn you** <note>original: *leornadægie*</note>; sometimes ***i*** is used as the connecting vowel—**know you** <note>original: *cunige* in L., *cunnoge* in R., Mark 4:13</note>.

From verbs following the pattern of **to love** <note>original: *lufigan*</note>, a command <note>The imperative mood</note> is formed by dropping the ending ***-an***—**honour** <note>original: *arig* in L., Matthew 19:19</note>; **behold** <note>original: *sceawig* in L., Mark 13:1</note>.

In the past participle <note>The "done" form of a verb, such as "sent"</note>, the final ***d*** is sometimes changed to a ***t***—**set in** <note>original: *geinsettet* in the Argument to John, p. 2, l. 1</note>; **sent** <note>original: *asendet* in L., John 1:24</note>.

<summary>This page details specific grammatical variations in verb endings found in Northern Old English manuscripts, including how past tense and command forms differ from the standard West-Saxon dialect.</summary>
<keywords>inflexion, past tense, West-Saxon, Old English, linguistics, Lindisfarne Gospels, Rushworth Gospels, verb endings, Northumbrian dialect</keywords>

<gloss>that where the Lord was invited, the wine of the wedding-feast should fail, so that with the old things changed, all the new things which...</gloss>

<note>**Translator's Vocabulary Note:**
**Ihs/Hæt**: Abbreviations for Jesus. *Hæt* stands for *Hælend*, the Old English word for "Healer" or "Savior."
**Sps/Gast**: Terms for the Holy Spirit.
**Sunu monnes**: Literal translation of "Son of Man."
**Rushworth**: Refers to the Rushworth Gospels, an 8th-century manuscript.
**Eth (ð), Thorn (þ), Wynn (p)**: These are special Old English letters. *Eth* and *Thorn* represent the "th" sound; *Wynn* (which looks like a modern 'p') represents the "w" sound.</note>

[33] A little time yet I am with you and go to him who sent me. [34] You seek me and do not find me and where I am or will be, you cannot come. [35] Therefore the Jews said to themselves, "Whither is this man going, because we did not find him? Will he go to the dispersion of the heathens and teach the heathens?" [36] What is this word that he said, "You seek me and do not find me and where I am you cannot come"? [37] On the last day, however, the great day of the feast, the Savior <note>original: "se Hæt"</note> stood and cried out, saying, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. [38] He who believes in me, as the scripture says, streams shall flow from his belly living."

## RUSHWORTH.

From the part of the devil you are and the will of your father you will to work. He was a manslayer from the beginning and in truth he did not stand, therefore there is no truth in him when he speaks a lie; from his own things he speaks, for he is a liar and his father. [45] I however, who speak the truth, you do not believe me. [46] Which of you convicts me of sins? If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me? [47] Therefore, he who is from God hears the word of God; for that reason you did not hear, because you are not from God. [48] Then the Jews answered and said to him: "Did we not bless ourselves [by saying] that you are a Samaritan and have a devil?"

### RUSHWORTH.
<note>The Rushworth Gospels, also known as the MacRegol Gospels, contain a similar interlinear Old English gloss, though in a Mercian dialect rather than the Northumbrian of Lindisfarne.</note>

[25] there are truly and many others which the Savior performed which here are written; for my part, I do not think that the world could receive those books which are written. end amen.

The following note occurs at the end of the Gospel of St. John in the Rushworth book: "He who uses me <note>the scribe personifies the book here</note>, pray for Owun who glossed <note>provided the interlinear translation for</note> this book. Færmen the priest at Harewood <note>a village in West Yorkshire</note> has now written this book; use it with goodwill always, with true faith; peace is dearest to everyone."

<summary>This page contains the final verse of the Gospel of John and the formal conclusion of the text, followed by a personal colophon from the scribes Owun and Farman. These notes are vital for historians as they provide the names and locations of the Anglo-Saxon translators.</summary>

✠ Eadfrith, Bishop of the church of Lindisfarne, he wrote this book at the beginning, for God and for Saint Cuthbert <note>the patron saint of the Northumbrian church</note> and all the saints who are collectively on the island. And Ethilwald, Bishop of the Lindisfarne-islanders, pressed it out and bound it, as he well knew how to do. And Billfrith the anchorite <note>a religious recluse</note>, he smithied the ornaments that are on the outside, and adorned it with gold and with gems, and also with silver gilded over—pure wealth. And Aldred, an unworthy and most miserable priest, with God’s help and Saint Cuthbert’s, glossed it <note>wrote the interlinear translation</note> in English, and made himself at home with the three parts. Matthew’s part for God and Saint Cuthbert. Mark’s part for the Bishop. And Luke’s part for the community, and eight <term>ora</term> <note>a unit of currency or weight, likely silver</note> of silver as an entry fee. And Saint John’s part for himself <insert>I</insert> <note>the scribe originally wrote "ic" (I) but partially erased it</note> <margin>for his soul</margin> and four ora of silver with God and Saint Cuthbert, so that he might have acceptance through God’s mercy in heaven; happiness and peace on earth, progress and promotion, wisdom and sagacity through Saint Cuthbert’s merits. <margin>Born of Alfred, I am called Aldred; the son of Tilwin, a good woman, I speak excellently.</margin> ✠ Eadfrith, Ethilwald, Billfrith, and Aldred constructed or adorned this gospel for God and Cuthbert.

<term>Codex Rushworthiani</term> (The Rushworth Gospels): An 8th-century illuminated manuscript from Ireland, later brought to England.
<term>Macregol</term>: The high-king-like scribe and bishop of Birr who is credited with the stunning artwork and text.
<term>Evangelium</term>: The Latin term for Gospel, meaning "good news."
<term>Scriptori</term>: Latin for "the scribe."

<summary>This page contains a series of Latin verses characterizing the four Evangelists and their symbolic beasts, followed by a colophon identifying Macregol as the scribe and artist of the manuscript. It is a vital historical record that connects the manuscript to the Irish monastery of Birr in the early 9th century.</summary>
